content: Neuroblastoma is a rare and aggressive cancer that primarily affects infants and very young children. The tumors typically originate in the adrenal medulla and often present as an abdominal mass. High-risk neuroblastoma is characterized by metastatic disease and other features that increase the likelihood of poor outcomes. The rapid COJEC induction regimen involves administering higher single doses of specific chemotherapy drugs over a shorter treatment period, with reduced intervals between cycles. This approach increases the dose intensity of chemotherapy, which may potentially improve survival outcomes. The purpose of this study was to compare the efficacy and adverse effects of the rapid COJEC induction regimen with standard induction regimens in patients with high-risk neuroblastoma, as defined by the International Neuroblastoma Risk Group (INRG) classification system. The primary outcomes assessed were complete response, early toxicity, and treatment-related mortality. Secondary outcomes included overall survival, progression-free survival, event-free survival, late non-hematological toxicities, and health-related quality of life. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of electronic databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, up to November 11, 2014. Additional searches were performed in trial registries, conference proceedings, and reference lists of relevant articles. No restrictions were placed on publication year or language. The study included randomized controlled trials comparing the rapid COJEC regimen to standard induction regimens in high-risk neuroblastoma patients. Two independent reviewers selected studies, extracted data, and assessed the risk of bias. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. The analysis followed the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions, and the quality of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE framework, considering factors such as study limitations, consistency of results, imprecision, indirectness, and publication bias. The review identified one randomized controlled trial (CCLG-ENSG-5) involving 262 patients with high-risk neuroblastoma. Participants were randomized to receive either the rapid COJEC regimen (n = 130) or the standard OPEC/COJEC regimen (n = 132). The quality of evidence was rated as low due to concerns about risk of bias and imprecision. The study found no significant differences between the two treatment groups in terms of complete response (risk ratio [RR] 0.99, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.71 to 1.38), treatment-related mortality (RR 1.21, 95% CI 0.33 to 4.39), overall survival (hazard ratio [HR] 0.83, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.10), or event-free survival (HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.13). Early toxicities during pre-operative chemotherapy were assessed, including febrile neutropenia (two or more episodes), proven fungal infections, septicemia (one or more episodes), grade 3 or 4 gastrointestinal toxicity, renal toxicity (glomerular filtration rate < 80 mL/min/1.73 m²), grade 3 or 4 neurological toxicity, and ototoxicity (Brock grade 2 to 4). Statistically significant differences favoring the standard treatment arm were observed for febrile neutropenia, septicemia, and renal toxicity. For all other early toxicities, no significant differences were identified between the treatment groups. Late non-hematological toxicities were evaluated after a median follow-up of 12.7 years (range: 6.9 to 16.5 years). These included any complications, renal toxicity (glomerular filtration rate < 80 mL/min/1.73 m²), ototoxicity (Brock grade 1 to 4), endocrine complications, neurocognitive complications (e.g., behavioral, speech, or learning difficulties), and second malignancies. Statistically significant differences favoring the rapid COJEC arm were found for endocrine and neurocognitive complications. For all other late toxicities, no significant differences were observed between the treatment groups. The study did not report data on progression-free survival or health-related quality of life. The authors concluded that there was no clear evidence of differences in complete response, treatment-related mortality, overall survival, or event-free survival between the rapid COJEC and standard induction regimens. The lack of significant findings may be attributed to the low statistical power of the study or the relatively short follow-up period. Results regarding early and late toxicities were mixed. It is important to note that this trial was conducted in the 1990s, and since then, there have been significant advancements in treatment protocols and risk classification systems. Consequently, the current evidence is insufficient to draw definitive conclusions about the relative benefits and risks of the rapid COJEC regimen compared to standard induction therapy in high-risk neuroblastoma patients. Further research is necessary to provide more conclusive evidence.
